en.title: The King Who Came in Peace
story: Every year, thousands of Jewish families travelled to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. This year, there was extra excitement in the air. Jesus of Nazareth was coming, the teacher who had healed the sick and even raised Lazarus from the dead! Could He be the promised King?
As Jesus approached the Mount of Olives, He sent two disciples into a village to fetch a young donkey that no one had ever ridden. Everything happened exactly as He said.

Jesus’ choice of a donkey was very deliberate. Five hundred years earlier, the prophet Zechariah had written: ‘Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey.’ A conquering general would ride a war horse. A king who came in peace rode a donkey.

The crowd spread their cloaks on the road and waved palm branches, a symbol of victory. They shouted words from Psalm 118: ‘Hosanna! Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!’
Some Pharisees told Jesus to make His followers be quiet. Jesus answered, ‘If they keep quiet, the stones will cry out!’

Then something surprising happened. As Jesus came near and saw the city, He wept over it. ‘If you, even you, had only known on this day what would bring you peace!’ Many in the crowd wanted a king who would fight the Romans. Jesus came to do something far greater: to make peace between people and God.
Within a week, some of the same voices would shout ‘Crucify Him!’ But Jesus kept walking towards Jerusalem, because He had come to save.

verse.text: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!

lessons: Jesus is a humble King who comes in peace, not to conquer.
Jesus fulfilled the prophecies spoken about Him long before.
Jesus cares deeply about people, even those who don’t understand Him.
questions: Why did Jesus ride a donkey rather than a horse?
Why do you think Jesus wept over Jerusalem?
What kind of King do you need Jesus to be in your life?
en.listen: Be still for one minute. Imagine standing by the road as Jesus rides past. Ask Him: ‘What do you want to be King over in my life?’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Hosanna, Jesus, my King!
I welcome you as King over…
Thank you for coming to bring me peace with God.

mission.text: This week, choose peace instead of a fight, like the King who rode a donkey.

en.journal: Read Zechariah 9:9. Write down every word that describes the King, and how Jesus fulfilled it.

af.title: Die Koning wat in Vrede Gekom Het
story: Elke jaar het duisende Joodse families na Jerusalem gereis vir die Paasfees. Hierdie jaar was daar ekstra opgewondenheid in die lug. Jesus van Nasaret was op pad, die leermeester wat siekes genees en selfs Lasarus uit die dood opgewek het! Kon Hy die beloofde Koning wees?
Toe Jesus naby die Olyfberg kom, het Hy twee dissipels na ’n dorpie gestuur om ’n jong donkie te gaan haal waarop nog niemand gery het nie. Alles het presies gebeur soos Hy gesê het.

Jesus se keuse van ’n donkie was baie doelbewus. Vyfhonderd jaar tevore het die profeet Sagaria geskryf: ‘Wees baie bly, Sion! Kyk, jou koning kom na jou toe, regverdig en oorwinnend, nederig en op ’n donkie.’ ’n Veroweraar sou op ’n oorlogsperd ry. ’n Koning wat in vrede gekom het, het op ’n donkie gery.

Die skare het hulle mantels op die pad oopgegooi en palmtakke gewaai, ’n simbool van oorwinning. Hulle het woorde uit Psalm 118 geroep: ‘Hosanna! Geseënd is die Koning wat kom in die Naam van die Here! Vrede in die hemel en eer in die hoogste hemel!’
Party Fariseërs het vir Jesus gesê om sy volgelinge stil te maak. Jesus het geantwoord: ‘As hulle stilbly, sal die klippe uitroep!’

Toe het iets verrassends gebeur. Toe Jesus nader kom en die stad sien, het Hy daaroor gehuil. ‘As jy maar net op hierdie dag geweet het wat vir jou vrede sou bring!’ Baie in die skare wou ’n koning hê wat teen die Romeine sou veg. Jesus het gekom om iets baie groters te doen: om vrede tussen mense en God te maak.
Binne ’n week sou party van dieselfde stemme ‘Kruisig Hom!’ skree. Maar Jesus het aangehou om na Jerusalem te loop, want Hy het gekom om te red.

verse.text: Geseënd is die Koning wat kom in die Naam van die Here! Vrede in die hemel en eer in die hoogste hemel!

lessons: Jesus is ’n nederige Koning wat in vrede kom, nie om te verower nie.
Jesus het die profesies vervul wat lank tevore oor Hom gespreek is.
Jesus gee diep om oor mense, selfs die wat Hom nie verstaan nie.
questions: Hoekom het Jesus op ’n donkie gery eerder as op ’n perd?
Hoekom dink jy het Jesus oor Jerusalem gehuil?
Watter soort Koning het jy nodig dat Jesus in jou lewe moet wees?
af.listen: Wees een minuut lank stil. Stel jou voor jy staan langs die pad terwyl Jesus verbyry. Vra Hom: ‘Waaroor in my lewe wil U Koning wees?’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Hosanna, Jesus, my Koning!
Ek verwelkom U as Koning oor…
Dankie dat U gekom het om vir my vrede met God te bring.

mission.text: Kies hierdie week vrede in plaas van ’n bakleiery, soos die Koning wat op ’n donkie gery het.

af.journal: Lees Sagaria 9:9. Skryf elke woord neer wat die Koning beskryf, en hoe Jesus dit vervul het.

en.title: What Kind of King?
story: Palm Sunday is the start of what Christians call Holy Week, the final days of Jesus’ life before the cross. All four Gospels record Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem, and almost a third of the Gospels focus on this one week. The writers knew this was the centre of the story.

Jesus’ entry was a carefully chosen, public claim. By riding into the city on a donkey, He was acting out Zechariah 9:9 in front of thousands of pilgrims who knew the Scriptures. He was saying, without words, ‘I am the King you have been waiting for.’

But notice what kind of King. Zechariah describes Him as ‘righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey’, and the next verse says He will ‘take away the chariots… and the war-horses’ and ‘proclaim peace to the nations’. This King wins not by violence but by peace.

The crowd’s response was enthusiastic. Palm branches had been a symbol of Jewish national victory since the Maccabees drove out a foreign army two centuries earlier. ‘Hosanna’ (‘Save us now!’) was a cry from Psalm 118. Many were hoping Jesus would lead a revolt against Rome. They wanted a king who would fix their political situation.

Jesus’ tears over Jerusalem reveal the gap between what they wanted and what they needed. ‘If you had only known on this day what would bring you peace.’ Their deepest problem wasn’t Rome; it was separation from God. Jesus came to deal with that, through the cross.

This raises an honest question for us. We, too, can want Jesus to be a certain kind of king, one who fixes our problems on our terms. But Jesus doesn’t fit our expectations; He exceeds them. He came not to give us what we want, but to give us Himself.
The crowd that cheered on Sunday would scatter by Friday. Following Jesus isn’t about the excitement of the crowd; it is about trusting Him when His way looks different from ours.

verse.text: See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey.

lessons: Jesus deliberately fulfilled prophecy to show He is the promised King.
Jesus is a King of peace who deals with our deepest need: separation from God.
Following Jesus means trusting Him even when His way differs from our expectations.
questions: What did the crowd hope Jesus would do? What did He actually come to do?
Why do you think Jesus wept even while the crowd was celebrating?
In what ways might you want Jesus to be a different kind of king than He is?
en.listen: Set a timer for two minutes. Ask Jesus: ‘What do I expect from you that is different from what you want to give me?’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Jesus, you are the King of peace.
I confess I sometimes want you to fix… my way.
I welcome you as King on your terms, not mine.

mission.text: This week of Easter, read one chapter of Luke 19–24 each day to walk through Holy Week with Jesus.

en.journal: Write about the difference between a crowd that cheers and a disciple who follows. Which do you want to be, and what would it cost?

af.title: Watter Soort Koning?
story: Palmsondag is die begin van wat Christene die Lydensweek noem, die laaste dae van Jesus se lewe voor die kruis. Al vier Evangelies skryf Jesus se intog in Jerusalem op, en byna ’n derde van die Evangelies fokus op hierdie een week. Die skrywers het geweet dit is die middelpunt van die storie.

Jesus se intog was ’n versigtig gekose, openbare aanspraak. Deur op ’n donkie die stad in te ry, het Hy Sagaria 9:9 uitgespeel voor duisende pelgrims wat die Skrif geken het. Hy het sonder woorde gesê: ‘Ek is die Koning vir wie julle gewag het.’

Maar let op watter soort Koning. Sagaria beskryf Hom as ‘regverdig en oorwinnend, nederig en op ’n donkie’, en die volgende vers sê Hy sal ‘die strydwaens… en die oorlogsperde wegneem’ en ‘vrede aan die nasies verkondig’. Hierdie Koning wen nie deur geweld nie, maar deur vrede.

Die skare se reaksie was geesdriftig. Palmtakke was ’n simbool van Joodse nasionale oorwinning sedert die Makkabeërs twee eeue tevore ’n buitelandse leër verdryf het. ‘Hosanna’ (‘Red ons nou!’) was ’n uitroep uit Psalm 118. Baie het gehoop Jesus sou ’n opstand teen Rome lei. Hulle wou ’n koning hê wat hulle politieke situasie sou regmaak.

Jesus se trane oor Jerusalem wys die gaping tussen wat hulle wou hê en wat hulle nodig gehad het. ‘As jy maar net op hierdie dag geweet het wat vir jou vrede sou bring.’ Hulle diepste probleem was nie Rome nie; dit was skeiding van God. Jesus het gekom om dit te hanteer, deur die kruis.

Dit bring ’n eerlike vraag na vore vir ons. Ons kan ook wil hê Jesus moet ’n sekere soort koning wees, een wat ons probleme op ons voorwaardes regmaak. Maar Jesus pas nie in ons verwagtinge nie; Hy oortref hulle. Hy het nie gekom om ons te gee wat ons wil hê nie, maar om ons Homself te gee.

Die skare wat Sondag gejuig het, sou teen Vrydag verstrooi wees. Om Jesus te volg, gaan nie oor die opwinding van die skare nie; dit gaan daaroor om Hom te vertrou wanneer sy weg anders lyk as ons s’n.

verse.text: Kyk, jou koning kom na jou toe, regverdig en oorwinnend, nederig en op ’n donkie.

lessons: Jesus het doelbewus profesie vervul om te wys Hy is die beloofde Koning.
Jesus is ’n Koning van vrede wat ons diepste behoefte hanteer: skeiding van God.
Om Jesus te volg, beteken om Hom te vertrou selfs as sy weg van ons verwagtinge verskil.
questions: Wat het die skare gehoop Jesus sou doen? Waarvoor het Hy eintlik gekom?
Hoekom dink jy het Jesus gehuil selfs terwyl die skare fees gevier het?
Op watter maniere wil jy dalk hê Jesus moet ’n ander soort koning wees as wat Hy is?
af.listen: Stel ’n tydhouer vir twee minute. Vra Jesus: ‘Wat verwag ek van U wat anders is as wat U my wil gee?’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Jesus, U is die Koning van vrede.
Ek bely dat ek soms wil hê U moet… op my manier regmaak.
Ek verwelkom U as Koning op u voorwaardes, nie myne nie.

mission.text: Lees hierdie Paasweek elke dag een hoofstuk van Lukas 19–24 om saam met Jesus deur die Lydensweek te stap.

af.journal: Skryf oor die verskil tussen ’n skare wat juig en ’n dissipel wat volg. Watter een wil jy wees, en wat sou dit kos?

en.title: A House of Prayer for All Nations
story: On Monday, Jesus went into the temple in Jerusalem. The temple had several courtyards. The outer one, called the Court of the Gentiles, was the only place where non-Jewish people were allowed to come and pray to God.

But that courtyard had been turned into a busy, noisy market. Traders sold animals for sacrifices, and money changers swapped foreign coins for the special temple coins, often charging unfair prices. It was hard for anyone, especially foreigners, to pray there.

Jesus was filled with holy anger. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the benches of those selling doves, and He wouldn’t let people carry goods through the temple courts. Then He taught them: ‘Is it not written: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations”? But you have made it a den of robbers.’
Jesus’ anger wasn’t selfish or out of control. It was love for people who were being blocked from God, and zeal for His Father’s house.
Then the courtyard changed. Matthew says that ‘the blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them.’ The place that had been about money became a place of healing.

And children started shouting, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ The chief priests were indignant. But Jesus quoted Psalm 8: ‘From the lips of children and infants you, Lord, have called forth your praise.’
Jesus wants nothing to stand in the way of people coming close to God. And He delights in the praise of children, including yours.

verse.text: My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations.

lessons: God wants nothing to block people from coming close to Him.
Jesus’ anger was love-driven, protecting people’s access to God.
Jesus welcomes and delights in children’s praise.
questions: Why was it especially unfair to have a market in the Court of the Gentiles?
What is the difference between Jesus’ anger and selfish anger?
What sometimes ‘clutters’ your time with God?
en.listen: Be still and ask Jesus: ‘Is there anything cluttering my heart that you want to clear out?’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Jesus, thank you that you made a way for everyone to come close to God.
Please clear away anything in my heart that blocks you, like…
Hosanna to the Son of David!

mission.text: This week, make a clutter-free ‘house of prayer’ space: a quiet corner where you pray each day.

en.journal: Write a ‘Hosanna’ prayer of praise to Jesus, like the children in the temple.

af.title: ’n Huis van Gebed vir Al die Nasies
story: Maandag het Jesus die tempel in Jerusalem binnegegaan. Die tempel het verskeie voorhowe gehad. Die buitenste een, die Voorhof van die Heidene, was die enigste plek waar nie-Joodse mense toegelaat is om te kom en tot God te bid.

Maar daardie voorhof is in ’n besige, lawaaierige mark verander. Handelaars het diere vir offers verkoop, en geldruilers het buitelandse munte vir die spesiale tempelmunte geruil, dikwels teen onregverdige pryse. Dit was moeilik vir enigiemand, veral buitelanders, om daar te bid.

Jesus was vol heilige toorn. Hy het die tafels van die geldruilers en die bankies van die duiweverkopers omgegooi, en Hy wou nie toelaat dat mense goed deur die tempelvoorhowe dra nie. Toe het Hy hulle geleer: ‘Staan daar nie geskryf nie: “My huis sal ’n huis van gebed vir al die nasies genoem word”? Maar julle het dit ’n rowerspelonk gemaak.’
Jesus se woede was nie selfsugtig of buite beheer nie. Dit was liefde vir mense wat van God weggekeer is, en ywer vir sy Vader se huis.

Toe het die voorhof verander. Matteus sê dat ‘die blindes en die kreupeles in die tempel na Hom gekom het, en Hy het hulle gesond gemaak.’ Die plek wat oor geld gegaan het, het ’n plek van genesing geword.
En kinders het begin roep: ‘Hosanna vir die Seun van Dawid!’ Die hoofpriesters was verontwaardig. Maar Jesus het Psalm 8 aangehaal: ‘Uit die mond van kinders en babas het U, Here, lof laat kom.’
Jesus wil hê niks moet in die pad staan van mense wat naby God kom nie. En Hy geniet die lof van kinders, ook joune.

verse.text: My huis sal ’n huis van gebed vir al die nasies genoem word.

lessons: God wil hê niks moet mense verhinder om naby Hom te kom nie.
Jesus se woede is deur liefde gedryf, om mense se toegang tot God te beskerm.
Jesus verwelkom en geniet die lof van kinders.
questions: Hoekom was dit veral onregverdig om ’n mark in die Voorhof van die Heidene te hê?
Wat is die verskil tussen Jesus se woede en selfsugtige woede?
Wat ‘versper’ soms jou tyd saam met God?
af.listen: Wees stil en vra Jesus: ‘Is daar iets wat my hart versper wat U wil uitruim?’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Jesus, dankie dat U ’n pad gemaak het vir almal om naby God te kom.
Ruim asseblief enigiets in my hart op wat U versper, soos…
Hosanna vir die Seun van Dawid!

mission.text: Maak hierdie week ’n opgeruimde ‘huis van gebed’-plek: ’n stil hoekie waar jy elke dag bid.

af.journal: Skryf ’n ‘Hosanna’-loflied aan Jesus, soos die kinders in die tempel.

en.title: Zeal for His Father’s House
story: Mark tells the temple story in a ‘sandwich’, wrapped inside another strange event. On the way into Jerusalem, Jesus sees a fig tree full of leaves but with no fruit, and He curses it. Then He clears the temple. The next morning, the disciples see the fig tree withered from the roots. The two stories interpret each other: the temple, like the tree, looked impressive but bore no real fruit of prayer, justice and welcome.

The temple’s Court of the Gentiles was meant to be the place where the nations could seek Israel’s God. Isaiah 56 had promised that God would bring foreigners to His holy mountain, ‘for my house will be called a house of prayer for all nations’. Instead, the space had become a marketplace. Whether through dishonest trading or simply by crowding out prayer, the system had become a barrier rather than a doorway.

Jesus’ actions were a prophetic sign, like the prophets of old acting out God’s message. He quoted Jeremiah 7, where God warned that people were treating the temple like a hideout, ‘a den of robbers’, assuming its religious activity would protect them while their hearts were far from Him.

This raises an important truth about anger. Jesus’ anger was righteous: directed at injustice and at things that kept people from God, not at personal inconvenience. Paul later writes, ‘In your anger do not sin.’ Not all anger is wrong, but most of our anger is about ourselves. Jesus’ was about others and about God’s glory.

After clearing the temple, Jesus filled it with what it was meant to have: healing for the blind and lame, and praise from children. The religious leaders were outraged by the children’s ‘Hosanna’. Jesus answered with Psalm 8, which in its original context is praise to God Himself. Jesus was accepting worship meant for God.

There is a further layer. Within a week, Jesus would replace the temple altogether. When He died, the curtain tore. Through Him, believers became God’s temple, the place where His Spirit lives. Paul asks, ‘Don’t you know that you yourselves are God’s temple?’ So the question becomes personal: what in my life needs clearing out, so that I can be a house of prayer?

verse.text: Don’t you know that you yourselves are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in your midst?

lessons: God’s house is meant to be a doorway for all nations, not a barrier.
Righteous anger is about injustice and God’s glory, not ourselves.
Through Jesus, believers become God’s temple, a house of prayer.
questions: How does the withered fig tree help explain the temple clearing?
How can you tell the difference between righteous anger and selfish anger in yourself?
If you are God’s temple, what might Jesus want to ‘clear out’?
en.listen: Set a timer for two minutes. Invite Jesus into the ‘temple’ of your life. Ask: ‘What tables need turning over?’ Write down what you sense, and ask for His help.
prayer: Jesus, thank you that your Spirit lives in me.
Clear out of my heart whatever blocks prayer, like…
Make me a house of prayer, and use me to welcome others to you.

mission.text: This week, notice anyone who might feel unwelcome at church or youth group, and help them feel at home.

en.journal: Read Isaiah 56:3–7. Write about God’s heart for outsiders, and how Jesus fulfilled it.

af.title: Ywer vir sy Vader se Huis
story: Markus vertel die tempelstorie in ’n ‘toebroodjie’, toegedraai in ’n ander vreemde gebeurtenis. Op pad na Jerusalem sien Jesus ’n vyeboom vol blare maar sonder vrugte, en Hy vervloek dit. Dan reinig Hy die tempel. Die volgende oggend sien die dissipels die vyeboom van die wortels af verdor. Die twee stories verklaar mekaar: die tempel, soos die boom, het indrukwekkend gelyk maar geen werklike vrugte van gebed, geregtigheid en verwelkoming gedra nie.

Die tempel se Voorhof van die Heidene was bedoel om die plek te wees waar die nasies Israel se God kon soek. Jesaja 56 het belowe dat God buitelanders na sy heilige berg sou bring, ‘want my huis sal ’n huis van gebed vir al die nasies genoem word’. In plaas daarvan het die ruimte ’n markplein geword. Of dit nou deur oneerlike handel was of eenvoudig deur gebed uit te druk, die stelsel het ’n versperring geword eerder as ’n deur.

Jesus se optrede was ’n profetiese teken, soos die profete van ouds wat God se boodskap uitgespeel het. Hy het Jeremia 7 aangehaal, waar God gewaarsku het dat mense die tempel soos ’n wegkruipplek behandel, ‘’n rowerspelonk’, en aanneem dat die godsdienstige bedrywighede hulle sou beskerm terwyl hulle harte ver van Hom was.

Dit bring ’n belangrike waarheid oor woede na vore. Jesus se woede was regverdig: gerig op onreg en op dinge wat mense van God weggehou het, nie op persoonlike ongerief nie. Paulus skryf later: ‘As julle kwaad word, moenie sondig nie.’ Nie alle woede is verkeerd nie, maar die meeste van ons woede gaan oor onsself. Jesus s’n het oor ander en oor God se eer gegaan.

Nadat Hy die tempel gereinig het, het Jesus dit gevul met wat dit veronderstel was om te hê: genesing vir die blindes en kreupeles, en lof van kinders. Die godsdienstige leiers was woedend oor die kinders se ‘Hosanna’. Jesus het met Psalm 8 geantwoord, wat in sy oorspronklike konteks lof aan God self is. Jesus het aanbidding aanvaar wat vir God bedoel was.

Daar is nog ’n laag. Binne ’n week sou Jesus die tempel heeltemal vervang. Toe Hy sterf, het die gordyn geskeur. Deur Hom het gelowiges God se tempel geword, die plek waar sy Gees woon. Paulus vra: ‘Weet julle nie dat julle self God se tempel is nie?’ So word die vraag persoonlik: wat in my lewe moet uitgeruim word, sodat ek ’n huis van gebed kan wees?

verse.text: Weet julle nie dat julle self God se tempel is en dat God se Gees in julle woon nie?

lessons: God se huis is bedoel om ’n deur vir al die nasies te wees, nie ’n versperring nie.
Regverdige woede gaan oor onreg en God se eer, nie oor onsself nie.
Deur Jesus word gelowiges God se tempel, ’n huis van gebed.

Hoe kan jy die verskil tussen regverdige woede en selfsugtige woede in jouself herken?

prayer: Jesus, dankie dat u Gees in my woon.

en.title: A House of Prayer
story: The next day, Jesus went into the temple, God’s house in Jerusalem. People came there from far away to pray and worship God.

But when Jesus walked into the big courtyard, it didn’t feel like a place of prayer at all. It was like a noisy market! People were selling animals and changing money, and some were cheating the visitors.

Jesus was upset, because they were stopping people from coming close to God. He turned over the tables of the money changers. Coins clattered everywhere! ‘It is written,’ Jesus said, ‘my house will be called a house of prayer, but you are making it a den of robbers.’
Then something beautiful happened. Blind people and people who couldn’t walk came to Jesus in the temple, and He healed them.
And the children started shouting and singing, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ The important leaders didn’t like it. ‘Do you hear what these children are saying?’ they grumbled.
Jesus smiled. ‘Yes! Haven’t you read: from the lips of children God has called forth praise?’
God wants everyone to be able to come close to Him, including children. Your prayers and your praise are precious to Him.

verse.text: From the lips of children and infants you, Lord, have called forth your praise.

lessons: God wants everyone to come close to Him.
God loves the praise of children.
Jesus cares about people who are hurting.
questions: Why was Jesus upset when He saw the market in the temple?
How did Jesus feel about the children singing?
prayer: Dear Jesus,
thank you that I can come close to you.
I love to praise you.
Hosanna to you, Jesus! Amen.

af.title: ’n Huis van Gebed
story: Die volgende dag het Jesus die tempel binnegegaan, God se huis in Jerusalem. Mense het van ver af daarheen gekom om te bid en God te aanbid.

Maar toe Jesus die groot voorhof inloop, het dit glad nie soos ’n plek van gebed gevoel nie. Dit was soos ’n lawaaierige mark! Mense het diere verkoop en geld geruil, en party het die besoekers verneuk.

Jesus was ontsteld, want hulle het mense verhinder om naby God te kom. Hy het die tafels van die geldruilers omgegooi. Munte het oral gekletter! ‘Daar staan geskryf,’ het Jesus gesê, ‘my huis sal ’n huis van gebed genoem word, maar julle maak dit ’n rowerspelonk.’
Toe het iets moois gebeur. Blindes en mense wat nie kon loop nie, het in die tempel na Jesus gekom, en Hy het hulle gesond gemaak.
En die kinders het begin roep en sing: ‘Hosanna vir die Seun van Dawid!’ Die belangrike leiers het nie daarvan gehou nie. ‘Hoor U wat hierdie kinders sê?’ het hulle gebrom.
Jesus het geglimlag. ‘Ja! Het julle nie gelees nie: uit die mond van kinders het God lof laat kom?’
God wil hê almal moet naby Hom kan kom, ook kinders. Jou gebede en jou lof is vir Hom kosbaar.

verse.text: Uit die mond van kinders en babas het U, Here, lof laat kom.

lessons: God wil hê almal moet naby Hom kom.
God is lief vir die lof van kinders.
Jesus gee om oor mense wat seerkry.
questions: Hoekom was Jesus ontsteld toe Hy die mark in die tempel sien?
Hoe het Jesus gevoel oor die kinders wat sing?
prayer: Liewe Jesus,
dankie dat ek naby U kan kom.
Ek prys U graag.
Hosanna vir U, Jesus! Amen.

mission.text: Sing of sê môre drie keer ’n ‘Hosanna’ vir Jesus: in die oggend, teen middagete en voor slaaptyd.

trait.en: Jesus is worth my very best

en.title: Extravagant Love
story: Two days before the Passover, the chief priests were secretly plotting how to arrest Jesus and kill Him. Meanwhile, in the village of Bethany, just outside Jerusalem, Jesus was at a dinner held in His honour.

John tells us that Martha was serving, and Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, was reclining at the table with Him. Then Mary, their sister, came in carrying an alabaster jar of pure nard, a perfume made from a plant that grows in the Himalayas.
She broke the jar and poured the perfume over Jesus’ head and His feet, and wiped His feet with her hair. ‘The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.’

Some of the guests, especially Judas, were indignant. ‘Why this waste? This perfume could have been sold for more than a year’s wages and the money given to the poor!’ John adds that Judas didn’t really care about the poor; he was a thief who stole from the money bag.

Jesus defended her: ‘Leave her alone. She has done a beautiful thing to me… She poured perfume on my body beforehand to prepare for my burial.’ Mary seemed to understand what the disciples didn’t: that Jesus was going to die. Her gift was an act of love and worship.
Then Jesus said something remarkable: ‘Wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her.’

Right after this, Mark tells us, Judas went to the chief priests to betray Jesus for money. The contrast is striking: Mary gave her most valuable possession to Jesus, while Judas sold Jesus for thirty silver coins.
What does our love for Jesus look like? Love that gives its best, even when others call it a waste, is beautiful to Him.

verse.text: Leave her alone… She has done a beautiful thing to me.

lessons: Jesus is worth our very best, even what others call a waste.
True worship gives generously from love.
Jesus notices and treasures acts of love towards Him.
questions: What did Mary seem to understand that the disciples didn’t?
How are Mary and Judas a contrast in this story?
What is something precious you could offer to Jesus?
en.listen: Be still and ask Jesus: ‘What would be a beautiful gift to you from me this week?’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Jesus, you are worth my very best.
I want to give you…
Thank you for noticing every act of love.

mission.text: This week, give something costly to Jesus: your time, a gift to someone in need, or a sacrifice of something you enjoy.

en.journal: Write about the most precious thing you have. What would it mean to offer it to Jesus?

af.title: Kwistige Liefde
story: Twee dae voor die Paasfees het die hoofpriesters in die geheim beplan hoe om Jesus gevange te neem en dood te maak. Intussen, in die dorpie Betanië, net buite Jerusalem, was Jesus by ’n ete wat ter ere van Hom gehou is.

Johannes vertel ons dat Marta bedien het, en Lasarus, wat Jesus uit die dood opgewek het, saam met Hom aan tafel was. Toe het Maria, hulle suster, ingekom met ’n albasterfles suiwer nardus, ’n parfuum gemaak van ’n plant wat in die Himalaja groei.
Sy het die fles gebreek en die parfuum oor Jesus se kop en sy voete uitgegooi, en sy voete met haar hare afgedroog. ‘Die huis was vol van die geur van die parfuum.’

Party van die gaste, veral Judas, was verontwaardig. ‘Hoekom hierdie vermorsing? Hierdie parfuum kon vir meer as ’n jaar se loon verkoop gewees het en die geld aan die armes gegee!’ Johannes voeg by dat Judas nie regtig oor die armes omgegee het nie; hy was ’n dief wat uit die geldsak gesteel het.

Jesus het haar verdedig: ‘Los haar uit. Sy het iets moois aan My gedoen… Sy het vooruit parfuum op my liggaam gegooi om dit vir my begrafnis voor te berei.’ Dit lyk of Maria verstaan het wat die dissipels nie verstaan het nie: dat Jesus gaan sterf. Haar geskenk was ’n daad van liefde en aanbidding.
Toe het Jesus iets merkwaardigs gesê: ‘Oral waar die evangelie in die hele wêreld verkondig word, sal wat sy gedoen het ook vertel word, tot haar gedagtenis.’

Net hierna, vertel Markus ons, het Judas na die hoofpriesters gegaan om Jesus vir geld te verraai. Die teenstelling is opvallend: Maria het haar waardevolste besitting vir Jesus gegee, terwyl Judas Jesus vir dertig silwermuntstukke verkoop het.
Hoe lyk ons liefde vir Jesus? Liefde wat sy beste gee, selfs as ander dit ’n vermorsing noem, is vir Hom pragtig.

verse.text: Los haar uit… Sy het iets moois aan My gedoen.

lessons: Jesus is ons allerbeste werd, selfs wat ander ’n vermorsing noem.
Ware aanbidding gee vrygewig uit liefde.
Jesus sien en waardeer dade van liefde teenoor Hom.
questions: Wat lyk dit of Maria verstaan het wat die dissipels nie verstaan het nie?
Hoe is Maria en Judas ’n teenstelling in hierdie storie?
Wat is iets kosbaars wat jy vir Jesus kan aanbied?
af.listen: Wees stil en vra Jesus: ‘Wat sou hierdie week ’n pragtige geskenk van my aan U wees?’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Jesus, U is my allerbeste werd.
Ek wil vir U… gee.
Dankie dat U elke daad van liefde raaksien.

mission.text: Gee hierdie week iets kosbaars vir Jesus: jou tyd, ’n geskenk aan iemand in nood, of om iets op te gee wat jy geniet.

af.journal: Skryf oor die kosbaarste ding wat jy het. Wat sou dit beteken om dit vir Jesus aan te bied?

en.title: A Beautiful Waste
story: Mark frames this story deliberately. It opens with the chief priests plotting to kill Jesus, and it closes with Judas agreeing to betray Him for money. In between, sandwiched by hostility and betrayal, is one of the most beautiful acts of devotion in the Gospels.
John identifies the woman as Mary of Bethany, the same Mary who had sat at Jesus’ feet listening while Martha served. Once again she is at His feet, this time not to learn but to worship.

The perfume was worth over 300 denarii, about a year’s wages for a labourer. It may have been Mary’s savings or her family’s security. She didn’t pour out a few drops; she broke the jar, which meant it could never be used again. This was total, irreversible devotion.

The objection sounds reasonable: ‘It could have been given to the poor.’ Concern for the poor is good and biblical. But Jesus exposes a false choice. ‘The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them any time you want. But you will not always have me.’ He is quoting Deuteronomy 15, which commands generosity to the poor, so He isn’t dismissing them. He is saying that this moment, right before His death, called for worship.

Jesus interprets her act as anointing His body for burial. In the ancient world, kings were anointed with oil at their coronation. Mary anoints the King, but for a coronation that would happen on a cross. Whether or not she fully understood it, she was honouring Jesus as the King who was about to die.
Then Jesus makes an extraordinary promise: her story will be told wherever the gospel goes. It is the only time Jesus said this about anyone.

Judas, by contrast, is the one who calculates. He sees waste in Mary’s love and profit in Jesus’ death. Mark’s placement of these two side by side asks every reader a question: are you counting the cost of devotion, or pouring yourself out in love?
Worship that holds nothing back can look foolish to observers. To Jesus, it is beautiful.

verse.text: Truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her.

lessons: Wholehearted devotion to Jesus is never a waste.
Worship and care for the poor aren’t rivals; both flow from love for Jesus.
Mary honoured Jesus as the King whose crowning would be the cross.
questions: Why does Mark place Mary’s story between the plot and Judas’ betrayal?
How does Jesus respond to the ‘give it to the poor’ objection without dismissing the poor?
Where are you tempted to ‘calculate’ your devotion to Jesus?
en.listen: Set a timer for two minutes. Imagine breaking your own ‘alabaster jar’ before Jesus. What is in it? Ask Him what He thinks of your love. Write it down.
prayer: Jesus, you are worthy of everything I have.
I want to stop calculating and pour out my love, especially…
Thank you that my love for you is beautiful to you.

mission.text: This week, do one act of ‘beautiful waste’ for Jesus: worship, generosity or service that costs you something.

en.journal: Write about the difference between Mary and Judas. What does each one value most? What do you value most?

af.title: ’n Pragtige Vermorsing
story: Markus raam hierdie storie doelbewus in. Dit begin met die hoofpriesters wat beplan om Jesus dood te maak, en dit eindig met Judas wat instem om Hom vir geld te verraai. Tussenin, toegedraai in vyandigheid en verraad, is een van die mooiste dade van toewyding in die Evangelies.

Johannes identifiseer die vrou as Maria van Betanië, dieselfde Maria wat by Jesus se voete gesit en geluister het terwyl Marta bedien het. Weer eens is sy by sy voete, hierdie keer nie om te leer nie, maar om te aanbid.

Die parfuum was meer as 300 denarii werd, omtrent ’n jaar se loon vir ’n arbeider. Dit was dalk Maria se spaargeld of haar familie se sekuriteit. Sy het nie ’n paar druppels uitgegooi nie; sy het die fles gebreek, wat beteken het dit kon nooit weer gebruik word nie. Dit was volkome, onomkeerbare toewyding.

Die beswaar klink redelik: ‘Dit kon aan die armes gegee gewees het.’ Om vir die armes om te gee, is goed en Bybels. Maar Jesus ontbloot ’n vals keuse. ‘Die armes het julle altyd by julle, en julle kan hulle help wanneer julle wil. Maar My het julle nie altyd nie.’ Hy haal Deuteronomium 15 aan, wat vrygewigheid teenoor die armes beveel, so Hy maak hulle nie af nie. Hy sê dat hierdie oomblik, net voor sy dood, aanbidding gevra het.

Jesus verklaar haar daad as die salwing van sy liggaam vir die begrafnis. In die antieke wêreld is konings by hulle kroning met olie gesalf. Maria salf die Koning, maar vir ’n kroning wat aan ’n kruis sou plaasvind. Of sy dit ten volle verstaan het of nie, sy het Jesus geëer as die Koning wat op die punt was om te sterf.
Dan maak Jesus ’n buitengewone belofte: haar storie sal vertel word oral waar die evangelie gaan. Dit is die enigste keer dat Jesus dit oor enigiemand gesê het.

Judas, daarenteen, is die een wat bereken. Hy sien vermorsing in Maria se liefde en wins in Jesus se dood. Markus se plasing van hierdie twee langs mekaar vra elke leser ’n vraag: bereken jy die koste van toewyding, of stort jy jouself in liefde uit?
Aanbidding wat niks terughou nie, kan vir toeskouers dwaas lyk. Vir Jesus is dit pragtig.

verse.text: Ek sê vir julle die waarheid: oral waar die evangelie in die hele wêreld verkondig word, sal wat sy gedoen het ook vertel word, tot haar gedagtenis.

lessons: Volhartige toewyding aan Jesus is nooit ’n vermorsing nie.
Aanbidding en sorg vir die armes is nie teenstanders nie; albei vloei uit liefde vir Jesus.
Maria het Jesus geëer as die Koning wie se kroning die kruis sou wees.
questions: Hoekom plaas Markus Maria se storie tussen die sameswering en Judas se verraad?
Hoe reageer Jesus op die ‘gee dit aan die armes’-beswaar sonder om die armes af te maak?
Waar kom jy in die versoeking om jou toewyding aan Jesus te ‘bereken’?
af.listen: Stel ’n tydhouer vir twee minute. Stel jou voor jy breek jou eie ‘albasterfles’ voor Jesus. Wat is daarin? Vra Hom wat Hy van jou liefde dink. Skryf dit neer.
prayer: Jesus, U is alles wat ek het, werd.
Ek wil ophou bereken en my liefde uitstort, veral…
Dankie dat my liefde vir U vir U pragtig is.

mission.text: Doen hierdie week een daad van ‘pragtige vermorsing’ vir Jesus: aanbidding, vrygewigheid of diens wat jou iets kos.

en.title: Mary’s Beautiful Gift
story: A few days before the cross, Jesus was having dinner with friends in the village of Bethany. Martha was serving the food, and Lazarus, whom Jesus had brought back to life, was at the table.
Then Mary came in, holding a beautiful jar. Inside was very expensive perfume called nard. It cost about as much as a worker earned in a whole year!
Mary broke the jar open and poured the perfume over Jesus’ head and feet. Then she wiped His feet with her hair. The whole house filled with the sweet smell.
Some of the people at the table were cross. ‘What a waste!’ they said. ‘That perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor!’

But Jesus said, ‘Leave her alone. She has done a beautiful thing to me.’ Mary loved Jesus so much that she gave Him her very best. And Jesus said that wherever the good news is told, people would remember what she did. And here we are, still telling her story!
Mary didn’t give Jesus her leftovers. She gave Him her most precious thing, because He was worth it. Jesus is worth our very best too: our love, our time and our hearts.

en.title: The New Covenant
story: Every year at Passover, Jewish families remembered the night God rescued their ancestors from slavery in Egypt. Each family sacrificed a lamb and painted its blood on their doorframes, and the angel of death ‘passed over’ those houses. Then God led His people out to freedom.

On Thursday evening of that final week, Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal in a large upstairs room. When evening came, Jesus reclined at the table with the Twelve. ‘I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,’ He told them.
Then Jesus did something that would change the meaning of the meal forever. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them: ‘This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me.’
After supper He took the cup: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.’

A covenant is a binding relationship, sealed with a promise. The old covenant was made at Mount Sinai with the blood of animals. But God had promised through Jeremiah, ‘I will make a new covenant… I will put my law in their minds and write it on their hearts… I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more.’

Jesus was saying that He was the true Passover Lamb. Just as the lamb’s blood saved the Israelites in Egypt, His blood, poured out on the cross, would rescue us from sin and death and bring us into a new relationship with God, written on our hearts.
Even at that table, Jesus knew Judas would betray Him. And yet He shared the bread and cup with all of them.
When we take Communion today, we remember Jesus’ sacrifice, we celebrate that we belong to God through Him, and we look forward to the day when we will eat with Him in His kingdom.

verse.text: This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.

lessons: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb who rescues us.
The new covenant brings forgiveness and God’s law written on our hearts.
Communion helps us remember Jesus’ sacrifice and celebrate belonging to Him.
questions: How does the first Passover in Egypt point to Jesus?
What is a covenant? What is new about the new covenant?
What do you think about when you see Communion at church?
en.listen: Be still and imagine sitting at the table with Jesus. Ask Him: ‘What do you want me to remember about you?’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Jesus, thank you for being my Passover Lamb.
Thank you for your new covenant, and for forgiving me for…
I will remember you.

af.title: Die Nuwe Verbond
story: Elke jaar met Pasga het Joodse families die nag onthou toe God hulle voorouers uit slawerny in Egipte gered het. Elke familie het ’n lam geslag en sy bloed aan hulle deurkosyne gesmeer, en die engel van die dood het by daardie huise ‘verbygegaan’. Toe het God sy volk na vryheid uitgelei.

Donderdagaand van daardie laaste week het Jesus vir Petrus en Johannes gestuur om die Paasmaal in ’n groot bovertrek voor te berei. Toe dit aand word, het Jesus saam met die Twaalf aan tafel gaan sit. ‘Ek het baie daarna verlang om hierdie Paasmaal saam met julle te eet voordat Ek ly,’ het Hy vir hulle gesê.

Toe het Jesus iets gedoen wat die betekenis van die maaltyd vir altyd sou verander. Hy het brood geneem, gedank, dit gebreek en vir hulle gegee: ‘Dit is my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word; doen dit tot my gedagtenis.’
Ná die ete het Hy die beker geneem: ‘Hierdie beker is die nuwe verbond in my bloed, wat vir julle uitgegiet word.’

’n Verbond is ’n bindende verhouding, met ’n belofte beseël. Die ou verbond is by die berg Sinai met die bloed van diere gesluit. Maar God het deur Jeremia belowe: ‘Ek sal ’n nuwe verbond sluit… Ek sal my wet in hulle gedagtes sit en dit op hulle harte skryf… Ek sal hulle oortreding vergewe en nooit weer aan hulle sonde dink nie.’

Jesus het gesê dat Hy die ware Paaslam is. Net soos die lam se bloed die Israeliete in Egipte gered het, sou sy bloed, aan die kruis uitgegiet, ons van sonde en dood red en ons in ’n nuwe verhouding met God bring, op ons harte geskryf.
Selfs by daardie tafel het Jesus geweet Judas sou Hom verraai. En tog het Hy die brood en beker met almal gedeel.
As ons vandag Nagmaal gebruik, onthou ons Jesus se offer, vier ons dat ons deur Hom aan God behoort, en sien ons uit na die dag wanneer ons saam met Hom in sy koninkryk sal eet.

verse.text: Hierdie beker is die nuwe verbond in my bloed, wat vir julle uitgegiet word.

lessons: Jesus is die ware Paaslam wat ons red.
Die nuwe verbond bring vergifnis en God se wet op ons harte geskryf.
Nagmaal help ons om Jesus se offer te onthou en te vier dat ons aan Hom behoort.
questions: Hoe wys die eerste Pasga in Egipte na Jesus?
Wat is ’n verbond? Wat is nuut aan die nuwe verbond?
Waaraan dink jy as jy by die kerk Nagmaal sien?

prayer: Jesus, dankie dat U my Paaslam is.
Dankie vir u nuwe verbond, en dat U my vergewe vir…

en.title: The Lamb, the Bread and the Cup
story: To understand the Last Supper, you need to understand the Passover. In Exodus 12, God told each Israelite family to sacrifice a spotless lamb and put its blood on their doorframes. That night, judgement passed over every home marked by the blood. The Passover became Israel’s great annual festival of remembrance and identity: we were slaves, and God set us free.

Jesus chose this exact festival for His final meal and His death. That timing wasn’t accidental. John the Baptist had called Him ‘the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.’ Paul would later write, ‘Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.’

At the meal, Jesus reinterpreted two elements. The bread, ‘my body given for you’, pointed to His physical death, His body offered in our place. The cup, ‘the new covenant in my blood’, pointed to His life poured out to establish a new relationship between God and humanity.

Jeremiah 31 is the background. God promised a new covenant, different from the one at Sinai. Its features: God’s law written on hearts, not just on stone; personal knowledge of God (‘they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest’); and complete forgiveness (‘I will remember their sins no more’). The old covenant showed the standard; the new covenant brings transformation from within, through the Holy Spirit.

This is the heart of our faith. We don’t relate to God through a list of rules and repeated sacrifices, trying to stay acceptable. We relate to Him through Jesus’ once-for-all sacrifice, as forgiven children with hearts being changed by His Spirit. Obedience flows from that relationship, not towards it.

Luke records a sad irony: right after this, the disciples argued about which of them was the greatest. Jesus responded, ‘I am among you as one who serves.’ The new covenant community is marked by humble service, not status.

Paul tells us that whenever we eat the bread and drink the cup, ‘you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.’ Communion looks back to the cross, around at the community of believers, and forward to Christ’s return.

verse.text: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

lessons: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, and His death brings freedom from sin.
The new covenant brings hearts changed by the Spirit, personal knowledge of God and complete forgiveness.
Communion looks back to the cross, around at the church and forward to Jesus’ return.
questions: What three promises of the new covenant do you find in Jeremiah 31:31–34?
How is relating to God through the new covenant different from trying to earn His acceptance?
What does it mean that Communion ‘proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes’?

Thank you that you remember my sins no more, including…

af.title: Die Lam, die Brood en die Beker
story: Om die Laaste Avondmaal te verstaan, moet jy die Pasga verstaan. In Eksodus 12 het God elke Israelitiese familie gesê om ’n lam sonder gebrek te slag en sy bloed aan hulle deurkosyne te smeer. Daardie nag het die oordeel verbygegaan by elke huis wat met die bloed gemerk was. Die Pasga het Israel se groot jaarlikse fees van herinnering en identiteit geword: ons was slawe, en God het ons vrygemaak.

Jesus het presies hierdie fees vir sy laaste maaltyd en sy dood gekies. Daardie tydsberekening was nie toevallig nie. Johannes die Doper het Hom ‘die Lam van God wat die sonde van die wêreld wegneem’ genoem. Paulus sou later skryf: ‘Christus, ons Paaslam, is geslag.’

By die maaltyd het Jesus twee elemente ’n nuwe betekenis gegee. Die brood, ‘my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word’, het gewys na sy liggaamlike dood, sy liggaam wat in ons plek geoffer is. Die beker, ‘die nuwe verbond in my bloed’, het gewys na sy lewe wat uitgegiet is om ’n nuwe verhouding tussen God en die mensdom te vestig.

Jeremia 31 is die agtergrond. God het ’n nuwe verbond belowe, anders as die een by Sinai. Die kenmerke daarvan: God se wet op harte geskryf, nie net op klip nie; persoonlike kennis van God (‘hulle sal My almal ken, van die kleinste tot die grootste’); en volkome vergifnis (‘Ek sal nooit weer aan hulle sondes dink nie’). Die ou verbond het die standaard gewys; die nuwe verbond bring verandering van binne, deur die Heilige Gees.

Dit is die hart van ons geloof. Ons gaan nie met God om deur ’n lys reëls en herhaalde offers, terwyl ons probeer om aanvaarbaar te bly nie. Ons gaan met Hom om deur Jesus se eenmalige offer, as vergewe kinders met harte wat deur sy Gees verander word. Gehoorsaamheid vloei uit daardie verhouding, nie daarnatoe nie.

Lukas skryf ’n hartseer ironie op: net hierna het die dissipels gestry oor wie van hulle die grootste is. Jesus het geantwoord: ‘Ek is onder julle as een wat dien.’ Die nuwe-verbond-gemeenskap word gekenmerk deur nederige diens, nie status nie.

Paulus vertel ons dat elke keer as ons die brood eet en uit die beker drink, ‘verkondig julle die dood van die Here totdat Hy kom.’ Nagmaal kyk terug na die kruis, rondom na die gemeenskap van gelowiges, en vorentoe na Christus se terugkoms.

verse.text: Christus, ons Paaslam, is geslag.

lessons: Jesus is die ware Paaslam, en sy dood bring vryheid van sonde.
Die nuwe verbond bring harte wat deur die Gees verander word, persoonlike kennis van God en volkome vergifnis.
Nagmaal kyk terug na die kruis, rondom na die kerk en vorentoe na Jesus se terugkoms.
questions: Watter drie beloftes van die nuwe verbond kry jy in Jeremia 31:31–34?
Hoe verskil dit om deur die nuwe verbond met God om te gaan van om sy aanvaarding te probeer verdien?
Wat beteken dit dat Nagmaal ‘die dood van die Here verkondig totdat Hy kom’?
af.listen: Stel ’n tydhouer vir twee minute. Lees Jeremia 31:33–34 stadig. Vra God: ‘Wat wil U op my hart skryf?’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Jesus, my Paaslam, dankie vir u liggaam wat gegee is en u bloed wat vir my uitgegiet is.
Dankie dat U nooit weer aan my sondes dink nie, ook nie aan…
Skryf u weë op my hart, sodat ek U uit liefde gehoorsaam.

en.title: Bread and a Cup
story: On Thursday evening, Jesus and His twelve disciples met in an upstairs room in Jerusalem to eat the Passover meal together. Every year God’s people ate this meal to remember how God had rescued them from Egypt long ago.
But this Passover was different. Jesus knew it was His last supper with His friends before He went to the cross. ‘I have really wanted to eat this meal with you,’ He told them.
During the meal, Jesus took a flat loaf of bread. He thanked God for it, broke it into pieces and gave it to them. ‘This is my body, given for you,’ He said. ‘Do this to remember me.’

After supper, He took the cup of wine. ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you,’ He said. A covenant is a special promise, like an agreement of love that can’t be broken.
Jesus was telling them: ‘Tomorrow I will give my body and my life for you, so that your sins can be forgiven and you can be close to God forever.’
Today, when Christians share bread and wine (or juice) together at church, it’s called Communion or the Lord’s Supper. We remember Jesus and say thank you for His great love.

verse.text: This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me.

lessons: Jesus gave Himself for me.
Jesus made a new promise of love with us.
We remember Jesus when we share the bread and the cup.
questions: What did Jesus say the bread and the cup meant?
What does your church do to remember Jesus?
prayer: Dear Jesus,
thank you for giving your body and your life for me.
Thank you for your promise of love.
I will always remember you. Amen.

af.title: Brood en ’n Beker
story: Donderdagaand het Jesus en sy twaalf dissipels in ’n bovertrek in Jerusalem bymekaargekom om saam die Paasmaal te eet. Elke jaar het God se volk hierdie ete geëet om te onthou hoe God hulle lank gelede uit Egipte gered het.
Maar hierdie Paasfees was anders. Jesus het geweet dit was sy laaste aandete saam met sy vriende voordat Hy na die kruis gaan. ‘Ek wou regtig hierdie ete saam met julle eet,’ het Hy vir hulle gesê.

Tydens die ete het Jesus ’n plat brood gevat. Hy het God daarvoor gedank, dit in stukke gebreek en vir hulle gegee. ‘Dit is my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word,’ het Hy gesê. ‘Doen dit om My te onthou.’

Ná die ete het Hy die beker wyn gevat. ‘Hierdie beker is die nuwe verbond in my bloed, wat vir julle uitgegiet word,’ het Hy gesê. ’n Verbond is ’n spesiale belofte, soos ’n ooreenkoms van liefde wat nie gebreek kan word nie.
Jesus het vir hulle gesê: ‘Môre sal Ek my liggaam en my lewe vir julle gee, sodat julle sondes vergewe kan word en julle vir altyd naby God kan wees.’
Vandag, as Christene saam by die kerk brood en wyn (of sap) deel, word dit Nagmaal genoem. Ons onthou Jesus en sê dankie vir sy groot liefde.

verse.text: Dit is my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word; doen dit tot my gedagtenis.

lessons: Jesus het Homself vir my gegee.

dankie dat U u liggaam en u lewe vir my gegee het.

mission.text: Sê môre by ’n ete dankie vir Jesus dat Hy Homself vir jou gegee het.

story: On Thursday evening, Jesus and His twelve disciples met in an upstairs room in Jerusalem to eat the Passover meal together. Every year God’s people ate this meal to remember how God had rescued them from Egypt long ago.
But this Passover was different. Jesus knew it was His last supper with His friends before He went to the cross. ‘I have really wanted to eat this meal with you,’ He told them.
During the meal, Jesus took a flat loaf of bread. He thanked God for it, broke it into pieces and gave it to them. ‘This is my body, given for you,’ He said. ‘Do this to remember me.’

After supper, He took the cup of wine. ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you,’ He said. A covenant is a special promise, like an agreement of love that can’t be broken.
Jesus was telling them: ‘Tomorrow I will give my body and my life for you, so that your sins can be forgiven and you can be close to God forever.’
Today, when Christians share bread and wine (or juice) together at church, it’s called Communion or the Lord’s Supper. We remember Jesus and say thank you for His great love.

verse.text: This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me.

lessons: Jesus gave Himself for me.
Jesus made a new promise of love with us.
We remember Jesus when we share the bread and the cup.
questions: What did Jesus say the bread and the cup meant?
What does your church do to remember Jesus?
prayer: Dear Jesus,
thank you for giving your body and your life for me.
Thank you for your promise of love.
I will always remember you. Amen.

mission.text: Tomorrow, at a meal, say thank you to Jesus for giving Himself for you.

en.fact: The Passover meal had special foods: flat bread with no yeast, a roasted lamb, bitter herbs and cups of wine. Each one helped people remember the night God rescued Israel from Egypt.
en.deeper: Why do you think Jesus wanted His friends to remember Him with something as ordinary as bread?
en.journal: Draw bread and a cup on a table. Write: ‘Do this in remembrance of me.’

af.title: Brood en ’n Beker
story: Donderdagaand het Jesus en sy twaalf dissipels in ’n bovertrek in Jerusalem bymekaargekom om saam die Paasmaal te eet. Elke jaar het God se volk hierdie ete geëet om te onthou hoe God hulle lank gelede uit Egipte gered het.
Maar hierdie Paasfees was anders. Jesus het geweet dit was sy laaste aandete saam met sy vriende voordat Hy na die kruis gaan. ‘Ek wou regtig hierdie ete saam met julle eet,’ het Hy vir hulle gesê.

Tydens die ete het Jesus ’n plat brood gevat. Hy het God daarvoor gedank, dit in stukke gebreek en vir hulle gegee. ‘Dit is my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word,’ het Hy gesê. ‘Doen dit om My te onthou.’

Ná die ete het Hy die beker wyn gevat. ‘Hierdie beker is die nuwe verbond in my bloed, wat vir julle uitgegiet word,’ het Hy gesê. ’n Verbond is ’n spesiale belofte, soos ’n ooreenkoms van liefde wat nie gebreek kan word nie.
Jesus het vir hulle gesê: ‘Môre sal Ek my liggaam en my lewe vir julle gee, sodat julle sondes vergewe kan word en julle vir altyd naby God kan wees.’
Vandag, as Christene saam by die kerk brood en wyn (of sap) deel, word dit Nagmaal genoem. Ons onthou Jesus en sê dankie vir sy groot liefde.

verse.text: Dit is my liggaam wat vir julle gegee word; doen dit tot my gedagtenis.

lessons: Jesus het Homself vir my gegee.
Jesus het ’n nuwe belofte van liefde met ons gemaak.
Ons onthou Jesus as ons die brood en die beker deel.
questions: Wat het Jesus gesê beteken die brood en die beker?
Wat doen jou kerk om Jesus te onthou?
prayer: Liewe Jesus,
dankie dat U u liggaam en u lewe vir my gegee het.
Dankie vir u belofte van liefde.
Ek sal U altyd onthou. Amen.

mission.text: Sê môre by ’n ete dankie vir Jesus dat Hy Homself vir jou gegee het.

af.fact: Die Paasmaal het spesiale kos gehad: plat brood sonder suurdeeg, ’n gebraaide lam, bitter kruie en bekers wyn. Elkeen het mense gehelp om die nag te onthou toe God Israel uit Egipte gered het.
af.deeper: Hoekom dink jy wou Jesus hê sy vriende moet Hom onthou met iets so gewoons soos brood?
af.journal: Teken brood en ’n beker op ’n tafel. Skryf: ‘Doen dit tot my gedagtenis.’

en.title: Not My Will, but Yours
story: After the Last Supper, Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn and walked out of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley, to an olive grove on the Mount of Olives called Gethsemane.
Jesus took Peter, James and John with Him, and He began to be ‘deeply distressed and troubled’. ‘My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death,’ He said. ‘Stay here and keep watch.’

Going a little further, Jesus fell to the ground and prayed: ‘Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.’ The ‘cup’ was a picture from the Old Testament of suffering and of God’s judgement against sin. Jesus was about to take that judgement on Himself, for us.

Notice how honest Jesus was. He didn’t pretend to feel fine. He told His Father exactly how He felt. But He also trusted His Father completely. Luke says an angel came to strengthen Him, and He prayed so intensely that His sweat was like drops of blood.

Three times Jesus returned to find His disciples asleep. ‘Simon, are you asleep? Couldn’t you keep watch for one hour? Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.’

Then Judas arrived with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, and he betrayed Jesus with a kiss. Peter drew a sword, but Jesus stopped him and even healed the servant whose ear Peter had cut off. Then all the disciples fled.

Jesus’ obedience in Gethsemane wasn’t fear-based. He wasn’t afraid His Father would reject Him. It came from love and trust. Jesus said in John 14, ‘The world must learn that I love the Father and do exactly what my Father has commanded me.’ That’s the kind of obedience God invites us into: not trying to earn His love, but trusting Him because we are loved.

verse.text: Abba, Father… Yet not what I will, but what you will.

lessons: We can be completely honest with God about our feelings.
Jesus obeyed the Father out of love and trust, not fear.
Prayer gives us strength in the hardest moments.
questions: What was the ‘cup’ Jesus prayed about?
How did Jesus combine honesty and trust in His prayer?
Is there something hard God is asking you to do? How can you pray about it?
en.listen: Be still and tell God honestly about something hard you are facing. Then pray, ‘Not my will, but yours.’ Ask Him for strength, and write down what you sense.
prayer: Abba, Father, I trust you.
I feel… about…
Not my will, but yours be done.

mission.text: This week, when you are asked to do something hard, pray ‘Not my will, but yours’ and obey with love.

en.journal: Write your own Gethsemane prayer about something hard in your life: honest feelings, then trust.

af.title: Nie My Wil Nie, maar U Wil
story: Ná die Laaste Avondmaal het Jesus en sy dissipels ’n lofsang gesing en uit Jerusalem uit geloop, oor die Kidronvallei, na ’n olyfboord op die Olyfberg met die naam Getsemane.
Jesus het Petrus, Jakobus en Johannes saamgeneem, en Hy het ‘diep ontsteld en benoud’ begin word. ‘My siel is dodelik bedroef,’ het Hy gesê. ‘Bly hier en waak.’

’n Entjie verder het Jesus op die grond neergeval en gebid: ‘Abba, Vader, alles is vir U moontlik. Neem hierdie beker van My weg. Tog nie wat Ek wil nie, maar wat U wil.’ Die ‘beker’ was ’n prentjie uit die Ou Testament van lyding en van God se oordeel oor sonde. Jesus was op die punt om daardie oordeel op Homself te neem, vir ons.

Let op hoe eerlik Jesus was. Hy het nie gemaak of Hy goed voel nie. Hy het sy Vader presies vertel hoe Hy voel. Maar Hy het ook sy Vader heeltemal vertrou. Lukas sê ’n engel het gekom om Hom te versterk, en Hy het so intens gebid dat sy sweet soos druppels bloed was.

Drie keer het Jesus teruggekom en sy dissipels slapend gekry. ‘Simon, slaap jy? Kon jy nie een uur lank waak nie? Waak en bid sodat julle nie in versoeking kom nie. Die gees is gewillig, maar die vlees is swak.’

Toe het Judas aangekom met ’n skare gewapen met swaarde en knuppels, en hy het Jesus met ’n soen verraai. Petrus het ’n swaard uitgetrek, maar Jesus het hom gekeer en selfs die dienskneg genees wie se oor Petrus afgekap het. Toe het al die dissipels gevlug.

Jesus se gehoorsaamheid in Getsemane was nie op vrees gebaseer nie. Hy was nie bang sy Vader sou Hom verwerp nie. Dit het uit liefde en vertroue gekom. Jesus het in Johannes 14 gesê: ‘Die wêreld moet weet dat Ek die Vader liefhet en presies doen wat my Vader My beveel het.’ Dit is die soort gehoorsaamheid waarin God ons nooi: nie om sy liefde te probeer verdien nie, maar om Hom te vertrou omdat ons liefgehê word.

verse.text: Abba, Vader… Tog nie wat Ek wil nie, maar wat U wil.

lessons: Ons kan heeltemal eerlik met God wees oor ons gevoelens.
Jesus het die Vader uit liefde en vertroue gehoorsaam, nie uit vrees nie.
Gebed gee ons krag in die moeilikste oomblikke.
questions: Wat was die ‘beker’ waaroor Jesus gebid het?
Hoe het Jesus eerlikheid en vertroue in sy gebed gekombineer?
Is daar iets moeiliks wat God jou vra om te doen? Hoe kan jy daaroor bid?
af.listen: Wees stil en vertel God eerlik van iets moeiliks waarvoor jy staan. Bid dan: ‘Nie my wil nie, maar U wil.’ Vra Hom vir krag, en skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.

Ek voel… oor…

mission.text: As jy hierdie week gevra word om iets moeiliks te doen, bid ‘Nie my wil nie, maar U wil’ en gehoorsaam met liefde.

en.title: The Garden of Surrender
story: The Bible tells two garden stories that mirror each other. In the Garden of Eden, Adam faced a choice between God’s will and his own, and chose his own. In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus, whom Paul calls ‘the last Adam’, faced the same choice and said, ‘Not what I will, but what you will.’ Where the first Adam’s disobedience brought sin and death, the second Adam’s obedience would bring righteousness and life.

Gethsemane shows us the full humanity of Jesus. He was ‘deeply distressed and troubled’, His soul ‘overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death’. Luke, a doctor, records that His sweat was ‘like drops of blood falling to the ground’, a rare condition caused by extreme anguish. Hebrews says He prayed ‘with fervent cries and tears’. Jesus wasn’t pretending; the cross was truly terrible, and He felt its weight.

What was the ‘cup’? In the Old Testament prophets, it was a picture of God’s righteous judgement against sin (Isaiah 51, Jeremiah 25). Jesus wasn’t only facing physical pain. He was about to take the judgement our sin deserved, and experience separation from His Father, which He had never known.

Notice the word He uses: ‘Abba, Father’. In His deepest anguish, His prayer flows from intimate relationship. His obedience wasn’t the forced compliance of a slave or the fearful performance of someone trying to be accepted. It was the trusting surrender of a beloved Son. Hebrews says He ‘learned obedience from what He suffered’, not because He was ever disobedient, but because He experienced obedience at its costliest.

The disciples’ failure stands in contrast. Three times they slept. Then they fled. Jesus’ gentle words, ‘The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak’, recognise their good intentions and their weakness. He knew they would fail, and He went to the cross for them anyway.

At the arrest, Jesus remained in control. He healed the servant’s ear, rebuked violence and said this was happening ‘that the Scriptures would be fulfilled’. He wasn’t a victim; He was laying down His life willingly.
For us, Gethsemane shows what surrender looks like: radical honesty with God, combined with deep trust. You can tell God exactly how you feel and still say, ‘Your will be done.’

verse.text: During the days of Jesus’ life on earth, He offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears… and He was heard because of His reverent submission.

lessons: Jesus, the second Adam, chose the Father’s will where the first Adam chose his own.
Jesus’ obedience flowed from intimate love (‘Abba’), not fear or performance.
Surrender combines complete honesty with deep trust.
questions: How do the two gardens, Eden and Gethsemane, mirror each other?
What does Gethsemane reveal about Jesus’ humanity?
What is the difference between surrender out of trust and compliance out of fear?
en.listen: Set a timer for two minutes. Bring God the thing you find hardest to surrender. Tell Him honestly how you feel. Then, if you can, say, ‘Your will be done.’ Write down what you sense.
prayer: Abba, Father, thank you that Jesus chose your will for my sake.
Honestly, I struggle to surrender…
I trust you. Not my will, but yours be done.

mission.text: This week, practise ‘watch and pray’: set aside one evening for an extended time of honest prayer.

en.journal: Write about Romans 5:19: ‘Through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.’ How does Gethsemane show this?

af.title: Die Tuin van Oorgawe
story: Die Bybel vertel twee tuinstories wat mekaar weerspieël. In die tuin van Eden het Adam ’n keuse gehad tussen God se wil en sy eie, en hy het sy eie gekies. In die tuin van Getsemane het Jesus, wat Paulus ‘die laaste Adam’ noem, dieselfde keuse gehad en gesê: ‘Nie wat Ek wil nie, maar wat U wil.’ Waar die eerste Adam se ongehoorsaamheid sonde en dood gebring het, sou die tweede Adam se gehoorsaamheid geregtigheid en lewe bring.

Getsemane wys ons die volle menslikheid van Jesus. Hy was ‘diep ontsteld en benoud’, sy siel ‘dodelik bedroef’. Lukas, ’n dokter, skryf op dat sy sweet ‘soos druppels bloed was wat op die grond val’, ’n seldsame toestand wat deur uiterste angs veroorsaak word. Hebreërs sê Hy het ‘met harde roepstemme en trane’ gebid. Jesus het nie gemaak asof nie; die kruis was werklik verskriklik, en Hy het die gewig daarvan gevoel.

Wat was die ‘beker’? By die Ou-Testamentiese profete was dit ’n prentjie van God se regverdige oordeel oor sonde (Jesaja 51, Jeremia 25). Jesus het nie net liggaamlike pyn in die gesig gestaar nie. Hy was op die punt om die oordeel te dra wat ons sonde verdien het, en skeiding van sy Vader te ervaar, wat Hy nog nooit geken het nie.

Let op die woord wat Hy gebruik: ‘Abba, Vader’. In sy diepste angs vloei sy gebed uit ’n intieme verhouding. Sy gehoorsaamheid was nie die gedwonge nakoming van ’n slaaf of die angstige prestasie van iemand wat probeer om aanvaar te word nie. Dit was die vertrouende oorgawe van ’n geliefde Seun. Hebreërs sê Hy ‘het gehoorsaamheid geleer deur wat Hy gely het’, nie omdat Hy ooit ongehoorsaam was nie, maar omdat Hy gehoorsaamheid op sy duurste ervaar het.

Die dissipels se mislukking staan in teenstelling. Drie keer het hulle geslaap. Toe het hulle gevlug. Jesus se sagte woorde, ‘Die gees is gewillig, maar die vlees is swak’, erken hulle goeie bedoelings en hulle swakheid. Hy het geweet hulle sou faal, en Hy het tog vir hulle na die kruis gegaan.

By die gevangeneming het Jesus in beheer gebly. Hy het die dienskneg se oor genees, geweld bestraf en gesê dit gebeur ‘sodat die Skrif vervul kan word’. Hy was nie ’n slagoffer nie; Hy het sy lewe gewillig afgelê.
Vir ons wys Getsemane hoe oorgawe lyk: radikale eerlikheid met God, gekombineer met diep vertroue. Jy kan God presies vertel hoe jy voel en steeds sê: ‘Laat u wil geskied.’

verse.text: Toe Jesus nog hier op aarde was, het Hy gebede en smekinge met harde roepstemme en trane gebring… en Hy is verhoor omdat Hy Hom aan God onderwerp het.

lessons: Jesus, die tweede Adam, het die Vader se wil gekies waar die eerste Adam sy eie gekies het.
Jesus se gehoorsaamheid het uit intieme liefde (‘Abba’) gevloei, nie uit vrees of prestasie nie.
Oorgawe kombineer volkome eerlikheid met diep vertroue.
questions: Hoe weerspieël die twee tuine, Eden en Getsemane, mekaar?
Wat wys Getsemane oor Jesus se menslikheid?
Wat is die verskil tussen oorgawe uit vertroue en nakoming uit vrees?
af.listen: Stel ’n tydhouer vir twee minute. Bring vir God die ding wat jy die moeilikste vind om oor te gee. Vertel Hom eerlik hoe jy voel. Sê dan, as jy kan: ‘Laat u wil geskied.’ Skryf neer wat jy aanvoel.
prayer: Abba, Vader, dankie dat Jesus ter wille van my u wil gekies het.
Eerlik, ek sukkel om… oor te gee.
Ek vertrou U. Nie my wil nie, maar laat u wil geskied.

mission.text: Oefen hierdie week ‘waak en bid’: sit een aand opsy vir ’n langer tyd van eerlike gebed.

af.journal: Skryf oor Romeine 5:19: ‘Deur die gehoorsaamheid van een mens sal baie regverdig gemaak word.’ Hoe wys Getsemane dit?

en.title: Jesus Prays in the Garden
story: After supper, Jesus went to a garden to pray.
Jesus felt very sad, because He knew the cross was coming.
He prayed, ‘Father, I want what you want.’
Jesus obeyed His Father because He loves Him.
And He did it because He loves me too!

en.action: Kneel down, fold your hands and whisper: ‘Father, I love you.’
lessons: Jesus obeyed His Father because He loves Him.
questions: Can you kneel and pray like Jesus?
prayer: Dear Father,
I love you, and I want to do what you want. Amen.

story: Ná ete het Jesus na ’n tuin gegaan om te bid.
Jesus het baie hartseer gevoel, want Hy het geweet die kruis kom.
Hy het gebid: ‘Vader, ek wil hê wat U wil hê.’
Jesus het sy Vader gehoorsaam omdat Hy Hom liefhet.
En Hy het dit gedoen omdat Hy my ook liefhet!

verse.text: Nie wat Ek wil nie, maar wat U wil.

af.action: Kniel, vou jou hande en fluister: ‘Vader, ek het U lief.’
lessons: Jesus het sy Vader gehoorsaam omdat Hy Hom liefhet.
questions: Kan jy kniel en bid soos Jesus?
prayer: Liewe Vader,
ek het U lief, en ek wil doen wat U wil. Amen.

en.title: It Is Finished
story: After His arrest, Jesus was put on trial through the night. The Jewish council condemned Him for claiming to be the Son of God. The Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, found no basis for a charge against Him, but the crowd shouted, ‘Crucify Him!’ and Pilate gave in. Jesus was beaten, mocked and made to carry His cross towards a hill called Golgotha, ‘the place of the skull’.

There, the soldiers crucified Jesus between two criminals. Crucifixion was the cruellest punishment Rome used. Yet listen to Jesus’ words from the cross. For the soldiers: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ To one of the criminals, who asked to be remembered: ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.’ To His mother, He made sure she would be cared for by John.

From noon until three o’clock, darkness came over the whole land. Then Jesus cried out, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ In that moment, He was carrying the sin of the world and experiencing the separation that sin causes.

Finally, Jesus said, ‘It is finished,’ bowed His head and gave up His spirit. ‘It is finished’ translates one Greek word, ‘tetelestai’, which was written on receipts. It meant ‘paid in full’. The debt of our sin had been completely paid.

At that moment, the curtain of the temple, which separated the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt, from everyone else, was torn in two from top to bottom. God Himself had opened the way. Through Jesus, we can come boldly into God’s presence.
A Roman centurion who watched it all said, ‘Surely this man was the Son of God!’
Why is it called ‘Good Friday’? Because on the worst day in history, God did the best thing for us. Jesus took our place, so we could be forgiven and brought home to God.

verse.text: He Himself bore our sins in His body on the cross, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness.

lessons: Jesus died in our place, carrying our sins.
‘It is finished’ means the price for our sin has been paid in full.
The torn curtain shows that the way into God’s presence is open.
questions: What do Jesus’ words from the cross show about His heart?
What does ‘tetelestai’ (‘It is finished’) mean for you?
Why do you think the curtain tore from top to bottom?

af.title: Dit Is Volbring
story: Ná sy gevangeneming is Jesus deur die nag verhoor. Die Joodse raad het Hom veroordeel omdat Hy beweer het Hy is die Seun van God. Die Romeinse goewerneur, Pontius Pilatus, het geen grond vir ’n aanklag teen Hom gekry nie, maar die skare het geskree: ‘Kruisig Hom!’ en Pilatus het toegegee. Jesus is geslaan, gespot en gedwing om sy kruis na ’n heuwel met die naam Golgota, ‘die plek van die skedel’, te dra.

Daar het die soldate Jesus tussen twee misdadigers gekruisig. Kruisiging was die wreedste straf wat Rome gebruik het. Tog, luister na Jesus se woorde aan die kruis. Vir die soldate: ‘Vader, vergewe hulle, want hulle weet nie wat hulle doen nie.’ Aan een van die misdadigers, wat gevra het om onthou te word: ‘Ek sê vir jou die waarheid: vandag sal jy saam met My in die paradys wees.’ Vir sy ma het Hy gesorg dat Johannes na haar sou kyk.

Van twaalfuur tot drie-uur het duisternis oor die hele land gekom. Toe het Jesus uitgeroep: ‘My God, my God, waarom het U My verlaat?’ Op daardie oomblik het Hy die sonde van die wêreld gedra en die skeiding ervaar wat sonde veroorsaak.

Laastens het Jesus gesê: ‘Dit is volbring,’ sy hoof gebuig en sy gees gegee. ‘Dit is volbring’ vertaal een Griekse woord, ‘tetelestai’, wat op kwitansies geskryf is. Dit het ‘ten volle betaal’ beteken. Die skuld van ons sonde is heeltemal betaal.

Op daardie oomblik het die tempelgordyn, wat die Allerheiligste, waar God se teenwoordigheid gewoon het, van almal anders geskei het, van bo na onder in twee geskeur. God self het die pad oopgemaak. Deur Jesus kan ons met vrymoedigheid in God se teenwoordigheid kom.
’n Romeinse offisier wat alles dopgehou het, het gesê: ‘Hierdie man was regtig die Seun van God!’

en.title: The Torn Curtain
story: Christians have always placed the cross at the centre of their faith. Paul wrote, ‘I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.’ Why? Because the cross is where God’s love and justice meet.

Seven hundred years earlier, Isaiah had described a suffering servant: ‘He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on Him, and by His wounds we are healed.’ This is what theologians call substitution: Jesus took the place we deserved. He wasn’t a helpless victim; He laid down His life willingly, out of love.

Mark’s account is stark and deliberate. Jesus is mocked as ‘King of the Jews’, the very title that was true. Darkness covers the land at noon, a sign of judgement from the prophets. Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ That psalm begins in anguish but ends in triumph, declaring that future generations will proclaim ‘He has done it!’

John records Jesus’ final word: ‘tetelestai’, ‘It is finished.’ It was a word used for completed work, fulfilled obligations and debts marked ‘paid in full’. Nothing remains to be added to Jesus’ sacrifice. We cannot earn our salvation, and we don’t need to.

Then comes the detail that sums up everything: ‘The curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.’ This curtain, perhaps eighteen metres high, separated the Most Holy Place, the symbol of God’s presence, from the people. Only the high priest could pass through, once a year, with blood. Now it is torn open, from top to bottom, showing that God did it.

Hebrews explains what this means: ‘Since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way opened for us through the curtain, that is, His body… let us draw near to God with a sincere heart.’ Because of the cross, every believer has direct access to God’s presence, not through a priest or a ritual, but through Jesus.
The first person to make a full confession of faith after Jesus’ death in Mark’s Gospel is not a disciple but a Roman centurion: ‘Surely this man was the Son of God!’ The way is open to everyone.

verse.text: Since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near to God with a sincere heart.

lessons: At the cross, Jesus took the place we deserved, out of love.
‘It is finished’: nothing needs to be added to Jesus’ sacrifice.
The torn curtain means every believer has direct access to God’s presence.
questions: How does Isaiah 53 describe what Jesus did at the cross?
Why might Jesus have quoted Psalm 22, which ends in triumph?
How should knowing you have direct access to God change the way you pray?
en.listen: Set a timer for two minutes. Picture walking through the torn curtain into God’s presence. Draw near with confidence. Ask Him: ‘What do you want to say to me here?’ Write it down.
